stem: The chapter 'Nomadic Empires' deals primarily with the empire of the:
options: Mongols under Genghis Khan and his successors
solution: The chapter 'Nomadic Empires' deals primarily with the Mongols — a nomadic people of the Central Asian steppes who, under Genghis Khan and his successors, created one of the largest land empires in world history.

stem: The Mongols were originally a people of the:
options: Steppes (grasslands) of Central Asia, living as nomadic pastoralists
solution: The Mongols were originally a nomadic pastoralist people of the steppes (vast grasslands) of Central Asia (Mongolia). They lived by herding animals (horses, sheep, goats, cattle, camels) and moving with their herds, and they were also skilled horsemen and warriors — a way of life shaped by the steppe environment.

stem: The founder of the Mongol Empire, who united the Mongol tribes, was:
solution: The Mongol Empire was founded by Genghis Khan (originally named Temujin), who united the various warring Mongol and Turkic tribes of the steppe under his leadership in the early 13th century, and then led the Mongols in vast campaigns of conquest. He is regarded as one of the greatest conquerors in history.

stem: The name/title 'Genghis Khan' (Chinggis Khan) means approximately:
solution: The title 'Genghis Khan' (Chinggis Khan), which Temujin took when he was proclaimed the supreme leader of the Mongols (around 1206), is generally understood to mean something like 'universal ruler' or 'oceanic/universal Khan' — signifying his position as the supreme ruler of the Mongols and, in aspiration, of the world. The taking of this grand title reflected his supreme authority and the vast ambitions of the Mongol enterprise.

stem: Genghis Khan was proclaimed the supreme ruler of the Mongols at an assembly of chieftains in approximately:
solution: Genghis Khan (Temujin) was proclaimed the supreme ruler (Great Khan) of the Mongols at a great assembly (quriltai) of Mongol chieftains in approximately 1206. This marked the unification of the Mongol tribes under his leadership and the founding of the Mongol Empire, from which his campaigns of conquest were launched.

stem: The key military strength of the Mongols lay in their:
options: Fast, mobile cavalry (mounted horse-archers) and superb horsemanship, discipline, and military organisation
solution: The key military strength of the Mongols lay in their fast, highly mobile cavalry — mounted horse-archers who were superb horsemen and skilled with the bow — combined with iron discipline, effective military organisation, mobility, and tactics. The Mongols' cavalry could move with great speed over long distances, and their discipline, organisation, tactics (including feigned retreats and coordinated maneuvers), and later their adoption of siege techniques made them a formidable and successful military force, enabling their vast conquests.

stem: The Mongols organised their army on a decimal system, dividing troops into units of:
solution: The Mongols organised their army on a decimal system — dividing their troops into units of tens, hundreds, thousands, and ten-thousands (the ten-thousand unit being called a 'tumen'). This systematic decimal organisation, which cut across older tribal divisions and integrated men from different tribes into a unified structure, contributed greatly to the discipline, coordination, and effectiveness of the Mongol army, and it was an important element of Genghis Khan's military and administrative reforms.

stem: Under Genghis Khan and his successors, the Mongol Empire expanded to become:
options: One of the largest contiguous land empires in world history, stretching across much of Asia and into Europe
solution: Under Genghis Khan and his successors, the Mongol Empire expanded through vast campaigns of conquest to become one of the largest contiguous land empires in world history — stretching across much of Asia (including China, Central Asia, Iran, and parts of West Asia) and into eastern Europe (Russia). At its height, the Mongol Empire covered an enormous territory, bringing a huge area and diverse peoples under Mongol rule. The sheer scale of the Mongol conquests and empire is one of the most remarkable features of this period of history.

stem: Among the great civilisations conquered or attacked by the Mongols were:
options: China, the Islamic lands of Central and West Asia (including the Khwarazmian empire and later the Abbasid Caliphate), and Russia
solution: The Mongols conquered or attacked several of the great civilisations and states of Asia and eastern Europe, including: China (northern China under Genghis Khan, and later all of China under Kublai Khan, who founded the Yuan dynasty); the Islamic lands of Central and West Asia (including the powerful Khwarazmian empire, which Genghis Khan destroyed, and later the Abbasid Caliphate, whose capital Baghdad was captured and sacked in 1258); and Russia and parts of eastern Europe. These conquests brought vast and wealthy civilisations under Mongol rule or attack, and they had enormous consequences for the history of Asia and Europe.

stem: The Mongol conquest of China culminated in the founding of which dynasty by Genghis Khan's grandson Kublai Khan?
solution: The Mongol conquest of China culminated in the founding of the Yuan dynasty by Genghis Khan's grandson Kublai Khan, who completed the conquest of all China and ruled it as emperor. Under the Yuan dynasty, the Mongols ruled China; Kublai Khan established his capital at Dadu (near modern Beijing), and his court was famously visited by the Venetian traveller Marco Polo. The Yuan dynasty represents the Mongol rule of China and is an important example of a nomadic people conquering and ruling a great sedentary civilisation.

stem: After Genghis Khan's death, the vast Mongol Empire was:
options: Divided among his sons and descendants into several parts (khanates), which became increasingly independent over time
solution: After Genghis Khan's death (1227), the vast Mongol Empire was divided among his sons and descendants into several parts or 'khanates' (such as the Golden Horde in Russia, the Ilkhanate in Iran, the Chagatai Khanate in Central Asia, and the Great Khanate/Yuan in Mongolia and China). Initially these were parts of a single empire under a Great Khan, but over time the different khanates became increasingly independent and separate, and the unity of the empire gradually dissolved. This division of the empire among the descendants of Genghis Khan, and the subsequent evolution of the separate khanates, is an important feature of the later history of the Mongol Empire.

stem: The Mongols promoted trade and communication across their vast empire, which facilitated:
options: The movement of goods, people, and ideas across Asia (along routes like the Silk Road), linking East and West
solution: The Mongols promoted trade and communication across their vast empire, which — during the period of Mongol rule and relative peace (sometimes called the 'Pax Mongolica') — facilitated the movement of goods, people, and ideas across Asia, linking East and West. The unification of much of Asia under Mongol rule, and Mongol support for trade and secure communication (including a relay/postal system for messengers), made the great trans-Asian trade routes (like the Silk Road) safer and more active, promoting long-distance trade and the exchange of goods, technologies, ideas, and cultural influences between China, Central Asia, West Asia, and Europe. This Mongol-facilitated increase in trade and cross-cultural contact across Eurasia was one of the significant and more positive consequences of the Mongol Empire (alongside the destruction of the conquests).

stem: The Mongol relay/postal system for rapid communication across the empire was known as the:
solution: The Mongols established a highly effective relay/postal system, known as the 'yam', consisting of a network of relay stations (posts) at intervals along the routes of the empire, where messengers and officials could obtain fresh horses, food, and shelter. This yam system enabled rapid communication and the swift movement of messages, officials, and messengers across the vast distances of the Mongol Empire — an important administrative achievement that facilitated the governance, communication, and integration of the empire, as well as (indirectly) trade and travel. The yam relay system is a notable example of the administrative organisation and achievements of the Mongol Empire.

stem: Genghis Khan is credited with promulgating a code of laws/regulations for the Mongols, sometimes referred to as the:
options: Yasa (a body of Mongol laws and customs/regulations)
solution: Genghis Khan is credited with promulgating a body of laws, regulations, and customs for the Mongols, often referred to as the 'Yasa' (or Yasaq). The Yasa is understood to have been a code of Mongol laws and regulations — governing matters such as military organisation, discipline, administration, and social conduct — associated with the authority of Genghis Khan. The Yasa (whatever its exact original form and content, which is debated by historians) came to be regarded as embodying the law and customs of the Mongols as laid down by Genghis Khan, and it reflected his role not only as a conqueror but also as a law-giver and organiser who sought to give order, structure, and rules to the Mongol state and society. The tradition of the Yasa is an important aspect of the Mongol legal and political heritage associated with Genghis Khan.

stem: One important consequence of the Mongol conquests was that they:
options: Caused enormous destruction and loss of life in the conquered regions, but also (later) promoted trans-Eurasian trade, contact, and exchange
Only brought peace with no destruction
solution: The Mongol conquests had major and far-reaching consequences, which were mixed in character. On the one hand, the conquests caused enormous destruction, devastation, and loss of life in many of the conquered regions — cities were sacked and destroyed, populations were killed or displaced, and great damage was done to conquered civilisations (the Mongol conquests were often extremely violent and destructive). On the other hand, once the conquests were complete and Mongol rule was established over much of Asia, the resulting unification of a vast area under Mongol rule, and Mongol support for trade and secure communication, promoted trans-Eurasian (across Asia and into Europe) trade, contact, and the exchange of goods, technologies, ideas, and cultural influences between East and West on an unprecedented scale (the 'Pax Mongolica'). Thus, the Mongol conquests had both a destructive side (devastation and loss of life in the conquests) and a more constructive or connective side (the later promotion of trans-Eurasian trade, contact, and exchange under Mongol rule). This mixed and far-reaching impact is an important feature of the significance of the Mongol Empire in world history.

stem: The Mongols were generally, in matters of religion, relatively:
options: Intolerant, forcing everyone to convert to one religion
Tolerant, allowing the practice of various religions among their subjects and often not imposing their own beliefs
Only supportive of one religion everywhere
solution: The Mongols were generally, in matters of religion, relatively tolerant: they allowed the practice of various religions among their many subjects, and they often did not seek to impose their own beliefs (their traditional shamanistic/Tengrist beliefs) on the conquered peoples. Mongol rulers frequently patronised, consulted, or employed people of different faiths (including Buddhists, Muslims, Christians, and others), and religious diversity was generally tolerated within the empire. Over time, the Mongols in different parts of the empire themselves adopted the religions of the regions they ruled — for example, the Mongols (Ilkhanate) in Iran and (Golden Horde) in the western steppe eventually converted to Islam, while those in China (Yuan) were influenced by Buddhism and other faiths. This relative religious tolerance and the eventual adoption by the Mongols of the religions of their subject regions are notable features of the religious history of the Mongol Empire, and they reflect the pragmatic and adaptive character of Mongol rule over their diverse subjects.

stem: The historical study of the Mongols relies on sources written by:
options: The Mongols (like 'The Secret History of the Mongols') and, importantly, the many settled/literate peoples they conquered or dealt with (Chinese, Persian, Arab, European, and Russian writers)
solution: The historical study of the Mongols relies on a variety of sources — but importantly, most of the written sources about the Mongols were produced not by the Mongols themselves (who were originally a largely non-literate, nomadic people, though one important native source is 'The Secret History of the Mongols'), but by the many settled, literate peoples with whom the Mongols came into contact or whom they conquered — including Chinese, Persian, Arab, European (like the accounts of travellers such as Marco Polo and various missionaries and envoys), and Russian writers. These sources, written from various perspectives (often those of the conquered or of outside observers), provide much of the surviving information about the Mongols, their conquests, and their empire. Because many of these sources were written by the settled peoples who suffered from or feared the Mongol conquests, they often present the Mongols in a negative light (as destructive barbarians); historians therefore have to read the sources critically and from multiple perspectives to arrive at a balanced understanding of the Mongols and their empire. The nature and variety of the sources — mostly written by the settled peoples the Mongols encountered, rather than by the Mongols themselves — is an important consideration in the study of Mongol history, and it presents both opportunities and challenges for historians seeking to understand the Mongols and their impact.

stem: The significance of the Mongol Empire in world history lies partly in the fact that it:
options: Was one of the largest empires in history, created by a nomadic people, that reshaped much of Eurasia and promoted (after the conquests) unprecedented trans-Eurasian contact and exchange
solution: The significance of the Mongol Empire in world history is very great. It was one of the largest empires (and the largest contiguous land empire) in all of history, and it was remarkably created by a nomadic pastoralist people of the Central Asian steppes, under the leadership of Genghis Khan and his successors. The Mongol conquests and empire reshaped the political map and history of much of Eurasia — bringing China, Central Asia, Iran, West Asia, Russia, and other regions under or into contact with Mongol rule, destroying some states and civilisations and transforming others, and profoundly affecting the subsequent history of these regions. And, after the conquests, the unification of much of Asia under Mongol rule, together with Mongol support for trade and communication, promoted an unprecedented degree of trans-Eurasian contact, trade, and exchange of goods, technologies, ideas, and peoples between East and West (the 'Pax Mongolica') — greatly increasing connections across the whole of Eurasia. The Mongol Empire thus stands as a remarkable phenomenon in world history — a vast empire created by a nomadic people that reshaped Eurasia and greatly intensified the connections between its different parts — and it illustrates the important and sometimes underestimated role of nomadic peoples of the steppe in shaping world history. The chapter on 'Nomadic Empires' uses the Mongol Empire to explore the nature, achievements, and impact of a great nomadic empire, and to challenge simplistic views of nomads as merely destructive 'barbarians', showing instead their capacity for large-scale political organisation, conquest, administration, and the promotion of trans-continental contact and exchange.

stem: The way of life of the nomadic pastoralists of the steppe was shaped by:
options: The need to move with their herds in search of pasture, and the harsh steppe environment, which made them mobile, hardy, and skilled horsemen and warriors
solution: The way of life of the nomadic pastoralists of the steppe (like the Mongols) was shaped by their environment and mode of subsistence. Living in the vast grasslands (steppes) of Central Asia, they subsisted mainly by herding animals (horses, sheep, goats, cattle, camels), and they had to move regularly with their herds in search of pasture and water, according to the seasons — a nomadic (mobile) way of life. The harsh and demanding steppe environment, and this mobile, pastoral way of life, made the nomads hardy, self-reliant, mobile, and highly skilled as horsemen (the horse being central to their life and warfare) and as warriors. These qualities — mobility, hardiness, horsemanship, and martial skill — bred by their environment and way of life, were among the factors that made the steppe nomads such formidable warriors and conquerors when they were united and organised (as under Genghis Khan). The way of life of the steppe nomads, and how it shaped their character and capabilities, is an important background to understanding the Mongols and their remarkable conquests, and it illustrates the relationship between environment, way of life, and historical role. Understanding the nomadic pastoralist way of life of the steppe helps explain the character and the military and political achievements of the Mongols.

stem: The Mongols' adoption of siege warfare techniques (for attacking walled cities) was made possible largely by:
options: The skills and technology of engineers from conquered civilisations (such as Chinese and Persian engineers)
solution: The Mongols, who came from a nomadic steppe tradition of mobile cavalry warfare, initially lacked the techniques of siege warfare needed to capture strongly walled cities. Their acquisition and use of effective siege warfare techniques and equipment (such as catapults, siege engines, and other methods for attacking and breaching city walls) was made possible largely by their adoption and use of the skills, knowledge, and technology of engineers and specialists from the conquered civilisations — notably Chinese and Persian/Muslim engineers, whom the Mongols employed and relocated for this purpose. This adoption of siege technology and expertise from the conquered settled civilisations greatly enhanced the Mongols' military capabilities, enabling them to capture the walled cities and fortifications of the settled world, which their cavalry alone could not have taken. It is another example of the way in which the Mongols pragmatically made use of the skills, knowledge, and technology of the peoples they conquered to serve their own military and imperial needs, and of the mutual influence and adaptation between the nomadic conquerors and the settled civilisations. The Mongols' adoption of siege warfare from conquered engineers illustrates their adaptability and their effective use of the resources of the settled world, and it was an important factor in their ability to conquer the fortified cities and states of the settled civilisations.

stem: The traditional religion of the Mongols before their adoption of other faiths involved the worship of the Sky/Heaven and is described as:
options: Shamanism/Tengrism (worship of the Sky-god Tengri and nature spirits, with shamans)
solution: The traditional religion of the Mongols before they adopted other faiths was a form of shamanism/Tengrism — centred on the worship of the Sky or Heaven (the sky-god Tengri) and of nature and ancestral spirits, with religious specialists called shamans who communicated with the spirit world. This traditional shamanistic/Tengrist religion of the Mongols was later, in different parts of the empire, supplemented or replaced by the religions of the regions they conquered (Islam in the Ilkhanate and Golden Horde, Buddhist and other influences in China).

stem: The vast trans-Eurasian contact of the Mongol era also had the unintended consequence of facilitating the spread of:
options: Disease — notably, the Black Death (plague) is thought to have spread westward along the trade routes connected by the Mongol empire
solution: The vast trans-Eurasian contact, trade, and movement of people facilitated by the Mongol empire had, among its unintended consequences, the facilitation of the spread of disease across Eurasia — most notably, the Black Death (the great plague pandemic of the 14th century) is thought by many historians to have spread westward from Asia towards West Asia and Europe along the trade and travel routes that had been connected and made active by the Mongol empire. Thus, the same connections that promoted the beneficial exchange of goods, technologies, and ideas across Eurasia also, tragically, facilitated the spread of the devastating plague. This illustrates that the increased trans-continental contact of the Mongol era had unintended and harmful consequences (like the spread of disease) as well as beneficial ones, and it is an important example of how the increased connections of the Mongol era affected the wider world in complex ways. The role of the Mongol-era connections in facilitating the spread of the Black Death is a notable and sobering aspect of the wider impact of the trans-Eurasian contact promoted by the Mongol empire.

stem: The Venetian traveller who visited the court of Kublai Khan in China and left a famous account of his travels was:
solution: Marco Polo, the Venetian traveller, journeyed to Asia in the 13th century and spent many years at and in the service of the court of Kublai Khan (the Mongol emperor of China); his famous account of his travels described the wealth, cities, customs, and wonders of the Mongol empire and China, and it greatly influenced European knowledge of and interest in Asia. Marco Polo's travels illustrate the increased contact between East and West facilitated by the Mongol empire.

stem: The Mongol capture and sack of Baghdad in 1258 resulted in the end of the:
solution: The Mongol capture and brutal sack of Baghdad in 1258 (led by Hulagu, a grandson of Genghis Khan) resulted in the end of the Abbasid Caliphate, which had been the major political and religious institution of the Islamic world for centuries. The destruction of Baghdad and the killing of the caliph was a momentous and devastating event in Islamic history, marking the end of the Abbasid Caliphate and a major blow to the Islamic world. The region became part of the Mongol Ilkhanate (in Iran/Iraq).

stem: The Mongol khanate that ruled Russia and the western steppe was known as the:
solution: The Mongol khanate that ruled Russia and the western steppes (the region north of the Black and Caspian seas) was known as the Golden Horde. Under the Golden Horde, the Russian principalities were subjected to Mongol overlordship for about two centuries (the 'Mongol/Tatar yoke'), paying tribute to the Mongol khans. The Golden Horde was one of the major successor khanates into which the Mongol empire divided, and its rule had lasting effects on the history of Russia.

stem: The Mongol khanate established in Iran (Persia) was known as the:
solution: The Mongol khanate established in Iran (Persia) and the surrounding region (including Iraq) was known as the Ilkhanate, founded by Hulagu (a grandson of Genghis Khan) after his conquests in West Asia (including the sack of Baghdad in 1258). The Ilkhanid Mongols eventually converted to Islam and became patrons of Persian culture. The Ilkhanate was one of the major successor khanates of the Mongol empire.

stem: The great assembly of Mongol chieftains and leaders that met to make important decisions (such as choosing a new Great Khan) was called the:
solution: The great assembly of Mongol chieftains, princes, and military leaders that met to make important decisions — such as the election/proclamation of a new Great Khan, the planning of major campaigns, and other important matters of state — was called the 'quriltai' (or kurultai). The quriltai was an important institution of the Mongol state, reflecting an element of consultation and collective decision-making among the Mongol elite, and it was at a quriltai that Genghis Khan was proclaimed supreme ruler and that his successors were chosen. The quriltai is a notable feature of Mongol political organisation.

stem: The successor of Genghis Khan as Great Khan, under whom the Mongol conquests continued (including into Europe and China), was his son:
solution: The successor of Genghis Khan as Great Khan was his son Ogodei (Ogedei), who was chosen at a quriltai after Genghis Khan's death and under whom the Mongol conquests continued and expanded — including further conquests in China and the great Mongol invasion of Russia and eastern Europe (led by Batu and Subotai). Ogodei consolidated and extended the empire his father had founded, and the tradition of a Great Khan (initially based in Mongolia) as the supreme head of the whole Mongol empire continued for a time after Genghis Khan. Ogodei's reign was an important phase in the expansion and consolidation of the Mongol empire.

stem: Genghis Khan's campaign against the wealthy Khwarazmian empire (in Central Asia/Iran) was reportedly provoked by:
options: The mistreatment/killing of Mongol merchants and envoys by the Khwarazmians
solution: Genghis Khan's devastating campaign against the wealthy and powerful Khwarazmian empire (which ruled Central Asia and much of Iran) was reportedly provoked by the Khwarazmians' mistreatment — the killing and robbing — of Mongol merchants (a trade caravan) and then of the envoys whom Genghis Khan sent to seek redress. In response, Genghis Khan launched a massive and ferociously destructive campaign against the Khwarazmian empire, destroying its great cities (like Samarkand, Bukhara, and others) and conquering its territories. This campaign was one of the most destructive of the Mongol conquests, and it brought the rich lands of Central Asia and Iran under Mongol assault and rule. The episode illustrates both the importance the Mongols attached to trade and to the treatment of their envoys, and the terrible destructiveness of the Mongol conquests when provoked.

stem: The portable, felt-covered tents in which the Mongols and other steppe nomads lived were called:
solution: The Mongols and other steppe nomads lived in portable, felt-covered tents called 'yurts' (known to the Mongols as 'gers'). These round tents, made of a wooden frame covered with felt (made from the wool of their animals), were well suited to the nomadic way of life — they could be dismantled, transported, and reassembled as the nomads moved with their herds, and they provided shelter against the harsh steppe climate. The yurt/ger was the characteristic dwelling of the steppe nomads and remains in use in Mongolia today. It reflects the mobile, pastoral way of life of the steppe nomads and their adaptation to their environment.

stem: Genghis Khan's integration of men from different, formerly warring tribes into a unified army and state (cutting across old tribal loyalties) was significant because it:
options: Created a unified, loyal, and disciplined force whose loyalty was to Genghis Khan and the Mongol state rather than to individual tribes
solution: Genghis Khan's integration of men from different, formerly warring and rival tribes into a single, unified army and state — organised on the decimal system (units of tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands) that cut across and dissolved the old tribal divisions — was highly significant. It created a unified, disciplined, and loyal military and political force whose members' primary loyalty was directed to Genghis Khan and the Mongol state as a whole, rather than to their individual tribes and chieftains. This transcending of narrow tribal loyalties, and the integration of diverse tribes into a cohesive imperial structure loyal to the Khan and the state, was one of Genghis Khan's key achievements and a crucial factor in the unity, discipline, effectiveness, and success of the Mongol army and empire. It transformed a collection of fractious, warring tribes into a unified and formidable imperial power, and it illustrates Genghis Khan's genius not only as a military commander but also as an organiser and state-builder who forged a new kind of unity and loyalty among the Mongols. This achievement was fundamental to the rise and success of the Mongol empire.

stem: The period of relative peace and stability across Mongol-ruled Eurasia, which facilitated trade and travel, is sometimes called the:
solution: The period of relative peace, stability, and order across the vast expanse of Mongol-ruled Eurasia (during the height of the Mongol empire), which facilitated safe long-distance trade, travel, and communication across Asia (linking East and West), is sometimes called the 'Pax Mongolica' (the 'Mongol Peace'). During this period, the unification of much of Asia under Mongol rule, and Mongol support for and protection of trade and communication (including along the Silk Road and via the yam relay system), made travel and trade across Eurasia safer and more active than before, promoting an unprecedented flow of goods, people, technologies, and ideas between East and West. The 'Pax Mongolica' is thus used to describe the more positive, connective consequence of the Mongol empire — the promotion, once the conquests were over and Mongol rule established, of trans-Eurasian peace, trade, contact, and exchange. It parallels the concept of the 'Pax Romana' (the peace of the Roman empire). The Pax Mongolica is an important concept for understanding the impact of the Mongol empire on trans-continental connections and exchange.

stem: The Mongol rule over Russia (through the Golden Horde) is often referred to in Russian history as the:
solution: The period of Mongol rule/overlordship over the Russian principalities (through the Golden Horde), which lasted for about two centuries, is often referred to in Russian history as the 'Mongol yoke' (or 'Tatar yoke'). During this period, the Russian principalities were subjected to Mongol overlordship, paying tribute to the khans of the Golden Horde and acknowledging their supremacy, though they retained a degree of internal autonomy under their own princes. The 'Mongol yoke' had significant and lasting effects on the development of Russia — affecting its politics, economy, and society, and (in some interpretations) contributing to the later rise of Moscow and the character of Russian autocracy. The term 'Mongol yoke' reflects the Russian perception of this period as one of foreign domination and burden. The impact of Mongol rule on Russia is an important aspect of the wider consequences of the Mongol conquests and empire.

stem: Kublai Khan's attempts to invade and conquer which island country failed, partly due to storms (the 'kamikaze' or 'divine winds')?
solution: Kublai Khan (the Mongol emperor of China, of the Yuan dynasty) launched attempts to invade and conquer Japan, but these invasions failed — famously, in part, because the Mongol invasion fleets were destroyed by great storms (typhoons), which the Japanese called the 'kamikaze' ('divine winds'), seen as divine protection for Japan. The failure of the Mongol invasions of Japan (in 1274 and 1281) is a notable episode, illustrating both the ambitions and the limits of Mongol expansion (the Mongols, primarily a land power, struggled with naval invasions across the sea), and it holds an important place in Japanese history and legend (the 'kamikaze' becoming a powerful symbol). The failed invasions of Japan are an example of the boundaries of Mongol conquest.

stem: Under the Yuan dynasty in China, the Mongols made use of paper money, which was:
options: A Chinese innovation that the Mongols adopted and used in their administration of China
solution: Under the Yuan dynasty (Mongol rule in China), the Mongols made extensive use of paper money — a Chinese innovation (paper money had been developed in China before the Mongol conquest) that the Mongols adopted and used in their administration and economy of China. Marco Polo, among others, described with wonder the use of paper money in Kublai Khan's China. The Mongol adoption and use of paper money is an example of how the Mongols, in ruling the sophisticated civilisation of China, adopted and made use of Chinese institutions, technologies, and innovations (like paper money and Chinese administrative practices) in governing their Chinese domains. It illustrates the way in which the Mongols, as rulers of a great sedentary civilisation, adapted to and made use of the advanced systems of the peoples they conquered. The use of paper money under the Yuan dynasty is a notable example of this adaptation.

stem: Which of the following was a technology or idea whose spread across Eurasia was facilitated by the connections of the Mongol empire?
options: Technologies and knowledge (such as, according to many historians, gunpowder, printing, and other innovations) moving between East and West along the trans-Eurasian routes
solution: The connections and increased trans-Eurasian contact facilitated by the Mongol empire (the 'Pax Mongolica') are believed by many historians to have facilitated the spread of various technologies, knowledge, and ideas between East and West across the trans-Eurasian routes. Innovations and knowledge — such as (according to many historians) gunpowder, printing techniques, and other technologies and knowledge originating in China and the East — are thought to have spread westward (towards West Asia and Europe) during and after the period of the Mongol empire, carried along the trade and communication routes that the Mongol empire had opened up and made safer. Similarly, goods, techniques, artistic influences, and knowledge flowed in both directions across Eurasia. Thus, the Mongol empire, by unifying much of Asia and promoting trans-Eurasian trade and contact, is credited with facilitating an important increase in the exchange and diffusion of technologies, knowledge, and ideas between East and West — one of its significant and more constructive consequences for world history. (The exact routes and roles of the Mongol connections in specific cases are debated by historians, but the general facilitation of increased trans-Eurasian exchange by the Mongol empire is widely recognised.) This diffusion of technologies and knowledge across Eurasia, facilitated by the Mongol-era connections, is an important aspect of the impact and legacy of the Mongol empire.

stem: 'The Secret History of the Mongols' is significant as:
options: An important early source on Mongol history and Genghis Khan, produced within the Mongol tradition itself
solution: 'The Secret History of the Mongols' is significant as one of the most important early sources on Mongol history and on Genghis Khan (Temujin), produced within the Mongol tradition itself (it is the earliest surviving Mongol-language literary/historical work). Written not long after Genghis Khan's death, it provides an account (part historical, part legendary) of the origins and rise of Genghis Khan and the early Mongols. Because most written sources about the Mongols were produced by the settled peoples they conquered or encountered (Chinese, Persian, Arab, European), 'The Secret History of the Mongols' is especially valuable as a source that comes from within the Mongol tradition itself, offering a Mongol perspective on their own history and on Genghis Khan. It is thus an important and unique source for the study of the Mongols and of Genghis Khan, and it is used by historians alongside the many external sources. Its existence and significance illustrate the range of sources available for studying the Mongols and the value of having, alongside the external accounts, a source from within the Mongol tradition itself.

stem: The Mongols, as rulers of vast settled populations, increasingly had to:
options: Remain purely nomadic and ignore administration
Adapt to and adopt the administrative systems, institutions, and (often) the cultures and religions of the settled civilisations they ruled
solution: As the Mongols conquered and came to rule vast settled (sedentary) populations and great civilisations (like China, Iran, and Central Asia), they increasingly had to adapt to and adopt the administrative systems, institutions, practices, and (often) the cultures and religions of the settled civilisations they ruled — because ruling large, complex, settled societies required administrative structures, methods, and personnel that the Mongols' own nomadic traditions did not by themselves provide. Thus, the Mongols made use of the existing bureaucracies, administrative practices, and skilled officials of the conquered civilisations (Chinese, Persian, and others) to govern their settled domains; they adopted institutions and innovations of these civilisations (like paper money and administrative techniques in China); and over time the Mongols in different regions often adopted the religions (as the Ilkhanate and Golden Horde adopted Islam, and the Yuan were influenced by Buddhism) and, to varying degrees, the cultures of the peoples they ruled. This process of adaptation — the Mongols' adoption of the administrative systems, institutions, cultures, and religions of the settled civilisations they conquered, in order to rule them effectively — is an important feature of the history of the Mongol empire and of the transformation of the Mongols from purely nomadic conquerors into rulers of great settled empires. It illustrates the way in which nomadic conquerors, in ruling sophisticated sedentary civilisations, were themselves transformed and had to adapt, adopting much from the peoples they conquered. This dynamic of adaptation and mutual influence between nomadic rulers and settled subjects is an important theme in the history of nomadic empires like that of the Mongols.

stem: The rapid, disciplined mobility of the Mongol armies allowed them to:
options: Cover vast distances quickly, coordinate widely separated forces, surprise their enemies, and concentrate their strength where needed
solution: The rapid, disciplined mobility of the Mongol armies — based on their mounted cavalry (with each warrior often having several horses), their horsemanship, and their organisation and discipline — was one of their greatest military advantages. It allowed the Mongols to: cover vast distances with remarkable speed; coordinate the movements of widely separated armies and forces over great distances (achieving strategic coordination on a huge scale); surprise, outmaneuver, and outpace their enemies; rapidly concentrate their strength at decisive points; and pursue and harry defeated foes. This exceptional strategic and tactical mobility — the ability to move fast, far, and in a coordinated way — gave the Mongols a decisive edge over their more slow-moving, sedentary opponents, and it was fundamental to their military success and to the speed and scale of their conquests. The mobility of the Mongol armies, combined with their discipline, organisation, tactics, and skill with the bow, made them one of the most effective military forces in history, and it was a key factor in their ability to conquer such vast territories so rapidly. This military mobility and effectiveness is an important part of understanding how a nomadic people were able to create one of the largest empires in history.

stem: The decline and break-up of the unified Mongol empire into separate, increasingly independent khanates was due to factors including:
options: The vast size of the empire, difficulties of governing such an extent, succession disputes and rivalries among Genghis Khan's descendants, and the divergent development of the different khanates
The choice of the Mongols to disband
solution: The decline and break-up of the unified Mongol empire into separate, increasingly independent khanates was due to a combination of factors, including: the sheer vast size and extent of the empire, which made it extremely difficult to govern as a single unit and to maintain effective central authority over such enormous distances and diverse regions; succession disputes, rivalries, and conflicts among the numerous descendants of Genghis Khan (who claimed shares of and authority within the empire), which weakened its unity; the practice of dividing the empire among Genghis Khan's sons and their lines (creating the different khanates); and the divergent development of the different khanates, which — ruling different regions with different peoples, cultures, and interests, and often adopting the local religions and cultures (like Islam in the Ilkhanate and Golden Horde) — grew apart and increasingly pursued their own separate paths and interests. Together, these factors — the vast size and difficulty of governing the empire, succession disputes and rivalries among Genghis Khan's descendants, the division of the empire into khanates, and the divergent development of these khanates — led to the gradual weakening of the unity of the Mongol empire and its break-up into separate, increasingly independent, and eventually fully distinct khanates and states, which followed their own separate histories and eventually declined or were absorbed or transformed. The decline and fragmentation of the Mongol empire is an important part of its history, and it illustrates the difficulties of maintaining the unity of a vast empire, especially one divided among many heirs and spread across such diverse regions. Understanding the factors behind the decline and break-up of the Mongol empire completes the picture of its rise, height, and fall.

stem: The Mongol empire illustrates that nomadic peoples of the steppe could:
options: Not only conquer but also organise, administer, and rule vast empires, and profoundly shape the course of world history
solution: The Mongol empire powerfully illustrates that the nomadic peoples of the steppe were capable not only of conquest and destruction, but also of organising, administering, and ruling vast empires, and of profoundly shaping the course of world history. Far from being merely destructive 'barbarians' capable only of raiding and plunder (as they were often portrayed by the settled peoples who feared them), the Mongols, under Genghis Khan and his successors, demonstrated a remarkable capacity for large-scale political and military organisation (the decimal army, the integration of tribes, the yam relay system, the Yasa laws), for building and administering one of the largest empires in history (making use of the institutions and personnel of the settled civilisations they ruled), and for reshaping the political map and history of much of Eurasia and promoting trans-continental trade, contact, and exchange. The Mongol empire thus reveals the important, and sometimes underestimated, historical role and capabilities of the nomadic peoples of the steppe — their capacity not only to conquer but also to organise, administer, rule, and connect vast territories and diverse peoples, and to profoundly influence the wider world. This is one of the key insights and messages of the study of the Mongol 'nomadic empire', and it challenges simplistic and dismissive views of nomads, giving them their due place as significant actors and empire-builders in world history. The Mongol empire stands as the supreme example of the historical achievements and impact of a nomadic people, and it illustrates the important role of the steppe nomads in the history of Eurasia and the world.

stem: The horse was central to the life and success of the Mongols because it:
options: Was essential for their herding, mobility, and above all for their military power (mounted warfare), giving them speed, range, and striking power
solution: The horse was absolutely central to the life, way of life, and military success of the Mongols. As nomadic pastoralists, the Mongols depended on horses (among other animals) for their herding way of life, for transport and mobility across the vast steppe, and for products (like milk). Above all, the horse was the foundation of Mongol military power: the Mongols were superb horsemen, and their armies consisted of mobile cavalry — mounted warriors (horse-archers) — whose speed, range, mobility, and striking power on horseback gave them a decisive military advantage. Mongol warriors were trained to ride and shoot the bow from horseback with great skill from childhood, and each warrior often had several horses (allowing them to keep moving by switching mounts), giving the Mongol armies extraordinary mobility and endurance. The horse thus gave the Mongols the speed, range, mobility, and striking power that were fundamental to their military success and to the speed and scale of their conquests. The centrality of the horse to the Mongols — to their way of life and, above all, to their military power — is a key factor in understanding the Mongols and their remarkable achievements, and it illustrates the deep connection between the steppe way of life (centred on the horse) and the military and historical role of the steppe nomads. The horse was, in a real sense, the foundation of the Mongol empire.

stem: The Mongol practice of sometimes sparing skilled craftsmen, artisans, and useful people from conquered cities (while killing or enslaving others) reflects:
options: A pragmatic recognition of the value of skilled people, whom the Mongols used and relocated to serve their needs
solution: The Mongol practice of sometimes sparing skilled craftsmen, artisans, engineers, scholars, and other useful people from conquered cities (while killing, enslaving, or displacing much of the rest of the population) reflects a pragmatic recognition on the part of the Mongols of the value and usefulness of such skilled people. The Mongols, though often ferociously destructive in their conquests, recognised that skilled craftsmen, artisans, engineers (for example, those skilled in siege warfare and construction), scholars, and administrators were valuable and useful, and they frequently spared such people and relocated or deported them to serve the needs of the Mongols and their empire — for example, moving skilled craftsmen and engineers to work for the Mongols in other parts of the empire. This pragmatic exploitation of the skills and knowledge of conquered peoples — sparing and making use of the useful and skilled while destroying much else — is a notable feature of Mongol conquest and rule, and it also contributed (by relocating skilled people and their knowledge across the empire) to the trans-Eurasian diffusion of skills, techniques, and knowledge facilitated by the Mongol empire. It illustrates the mixture of destructiveness and pragmatic calculation in Mongol conquest, and the way in which the Mongols made use of the human and cultural resources of the peoples they conquered. This practice reflects the pragmatic and calculating side of Mongol conquest and rule, alongside its destructiveness.

stem: The overall assessment of the Mongols in the chapter seeks to move beyond the one-sided image of them as merely:
options: Destructive, savage 'barbarians', to a more balanced understanding of their organisation, achievements, and complex impact
solution: The overall assessment of the Mongols in the chapter seeks to move beyond the one-sided and largely negative image of them (common in many of the sources, written by the settled peoples who suffered from or feared the Mongol conquests) as merely destructive, savage, bloodthirsty 'barbarians' — an image that, while reflecting the real and terrible destructiveness of the Mongol conquests, is incomplete and one-sided. Instead, the chapter seeks to present a more balanced, rounded, and nuanced understanding of the Mongols — one that recognises not only the destructiveness of their conquests, but also their remarkable capacity for large-scale military and political organisation (the decimal army, the integration of tribes, the yam relay system, the Yasa laws), their achievement in building and administering one of the largest empires in history, their promotion (after the conquests) of trans-Eurasian trade, contact, and exchange (the Pax Mongolica), their pragmatic use of the skills and institutions of the peoples they conquered, and their complex and far-reaching impact on the history of Eurasia and the world. By moving beyond the one-sided image of the Mongols as mere destructive barbarians to this more balanced understanding of their organisation, achievements, and complex and many-sided impact, the chapter aims to give the Mongols their proper and rounded place in world history — recognising both the destructiveness and the constructive and connective achievements and impact of the Mongol empire, and challenging simplistic and dismissive stereotypes of nomads. This effort to reach a balanced and nuanced assessment of the Mongols, beyond the one-sided negative image, is an important aspect of the historical approach of the chapter, and it reflects the broader aim of understanding the past in a fair, balanced, and critical way, based on a careful and critical reading of the sources from multiple perspectives. This balanced assessment is part of the chapter's central purpose.

stem: The territory ruled by the Chagatai Khanate was located in:
solution: The Chagatai Khanate (named after Chagatai, a son of Genghis Khan) was the Mongol khanate located in Central Asia (roughly the region of former Soviet Central Asia and adjoining areas). It was one of the major successor khanates into which the Mongol empire divided, ruling the Central Asian heartlands of the former empire. The Chagatai Khanate, like the other khanates (the Golden Horde in Russia, the Ilkhanate in Iran, and the Yuan/Great Khanate in Mongolia and China), followed its own separate history after the fragmentation of the unified Mongol empire. Knowing the locations of the major khanates (Golden Horde in Russia, Ilkhanate in Iran, Chagatai in Central Asia, Yuan in China/Mongolia) helps in understanding the division and geography of the Mongol empire after its break-up.

stem: Genghis Khan died in which year, after which the empire passed to his successors?
solution: Genghis Khan died in 1227 (during a campaign), after which the leadership of the empire and the continuation of the conquests passed to his successors — first his son Ogodei (chosen as Great Khan) and then, in turn, to other descendants, while the empire was divided among his sons and their lines into the various khanates. Genghis Khan's death in 1227 marks the end of the career of the founder of the Mongol empire, but the empire he founded continued to expand and evolve under his successors for a long time afterward. The date of Genghis Khan's death (1227) is a key date in Mongol history, marking the transition from the founder to his successors.

stem: Which of the following best describes the composition of the Mongol armies as they expanded?
options: They consisted only of ethnic Mongols
They came to include large numbers of Turkic and other peoples of the steppe, and used the skills of various conquered peoples, alongside the Mongols
They were made up of Europeans
solution: As the Mongol empire and its armies expanded, the composition of the Mongol armies came to include not only the ethnic Mongols themselves, but also large numbers of Turkic and other peoples of the steppe (who shared a similar nomadic, horse-based, martial way of life and were incorporated into the Mongol military and political system), as well as, increasingly, the skills, forces, and personnel of various conquered peoples (for example, Chinese and Persian engineers skilled in siege warfare, and troops levied from conquered populations). Thus, the Mongol armies and empire were not purely 'Mongol' in a narrow ethnic sense, but incorporated and integrated many peoples — especially the Turkic and other steppe peoples, who were closely related to the Mongols in way of life and were absorbed into the Mongol enterprise, and also the skills and forces of the settled peoples the Mongols conquered. This incorporation and integration of diverse peoples — Turkic and other steppe nomads, and the skills and forces of conquered settled peoples — into the Mongol armies and empire was an important feature of the Mongol enterprise, and it contributed to the size, strength, and capabilities of the Mongol forces and to the multi-ethnic character of the empire. It also reflects the way in which the Mongol empire, like other great empires, drew upon and integrated the human resources of many different peoples. Understanding the diverse composition of the Mongol armies and empire gives a more accurate picture of the Mongol enterprise, which was a broad steppe-nomad and multi-ethnic phenomenon rather than a narrowly ethnic Mongol one.

stem: The trans-Eurasian trade routes that flourished under and were protected by the Mongols are collectively often known as the:
solution: The great trans-Eurasian overland trade routes that connected China and East Asia with Central Asia, West Asia, and Europe — and that flourished under, and were protected and promoted by, the Mongol empire during the 'Pax Mongolica' — are collectively often known as the 'Silk Road' (or Silk Routes). Named for the silk that was one of the important goods carried along them (from China to the West), the Silk Road routes carried a wide range of goods (silk, spices, precious stones, metals, textiles, and much more), as well as people, technologies, ideas, religions, and cultural influences, in both directions between East and West. Under the Mongol empire, which unified much of the length of these routes under a single power and provided security and support for trade and travel, the Silk Road trade and trans-Eurasian exchange flourished and intensified, promoting an unprecedented flow of goods, people, and ideas across Eurasia. The flourishing of the Silk Road under the Mongols is a key aspect of the trans-Eurasian trade, contact, and exchange facilitated by the Mongol empire, and it illustrates the connective, trade-promoting impact of the empire (the 'Pax Mongolica'). The Silk Road, and its flourishing under the Mongols, is thus an important part of the story of the impact of the Mongol empire on trans-continental trade and exchange.

stem: The study of the Mongols is valuable for world history because it illustrates:
options: Only the history of one small tribe
The important role of nomadic peoples and of Central Asia in world history, and the ways in which conquest, empire, trade, and cross-cultural contact have shaped the human past
solution: The study of the Mongols is valuable for world history because it illustrates several important and general themes and insights. It illustrates the important — and often underestimated — role of nomadic peoples (like the Mongols and other steppe nomads) and of Central Asia in world history: nomadic peoples were not marginal or merely destructive, but could create great empires, shape the destinies of settled civilisations, and act as significant agents of historical change and of connection across Eurasia. It illustrates the ways in which conquest and empire could reshape the political map and history of vast regions, for good and ill. It illustrates the role of trade, communication, and cross-cultural contact and exchange (promoted, in the Mongol case, by the unification of Eurasia and the Pax Mongolica) in connecting different civilisations and in the diffusion of goods, technologies, ideas, and peoples across continents. And it illustrates the dynamics of interaction, adaptation, and mutual influence between nomadic conquerors and the settled civilisations they ruled. In these and other ways, the study of the Mongols and their empire sheds light on important general themes and processes in world history — the role of nomads and of Central Asia, the nature and impact of conquest and empire, the importance of trade and cross-cultural contact, and the interaction of nomadic and settled peoples — and it offers a fascinating and instructive case study of a remarkable historical phenomenon. This general historical value and significance of the study of the Mongols — its illumination of important themes and processes in world history — is one of the reasons the Mongol empire holds an important place in the study of world history, and it is part of what makes the chapter on 'Nomadic Empires' valuable and illuminating. The Mongols thus offer not only a fascinating story, but also important insights into the workings and connections of the human past on a continental and world scale.

stem: Genghis Khan was proclaimed the supreme ruler of the Mongols at an assembly in the year:
solution: In 1206, at an assembly (quriltai) of Mongol chieftains, Temujin was proclaimed the 'Genghis Khan', the supreme ruler of all the Mongol tribes.

stem: The great assembly of Mongol chieftains that made important decisions, including choosing the Great Khan, was called the:
solution: The quriltai was the great assembly of Mongol chieftains and leaders, which met to take major decisions such as electing the Great Khan and planning campaigns.

stem: The Mongol conquest of China culminated in the founding of which dynasty by Kublai Khan?
solution: Kublai Khan, a grandson of Genghis Khan, completed the conquest of China and founded the Yuan dynasty (1271), ruling China as its emperor.

stem: The Venetian traveller who visited the court of Kublai Khan and wrote a famous account was:
solution: Marco Polo, a Venetian traveller, journeyed to China and spent years at the court of Kublai Khan; his account brought knowledge of the Mongol empire and the East to Europe.

stem: The Mongol capture and sack of Baghdad in 1258, led by Hulegu, resulted in the:
solution: In 1258 the Mongols under Hulegu captured and sacked Baghdad, killing the Caliph and ending the Abbasid Caliphate, a momentous event in Islamic history.

stem: The Mongol khanate that ruled Russia and the western steppes was known as the:
solution: The Golden Horde was the Mongol khanate that ruled over Russia and the western steppes for a long period, exercising authority over the Russian principalities.

stem: The Mongol khanate in Central Asia was named after Genghis Khan's son:
solution: The Chagatai Khanate, in Central Asia, was named after Chagatai, a son of Genghis Khan, and ruled the steppe and oasis regions of that area.

stem: The portable, felt-covered tents in which the Mongols lived were called:
solution: The Mongols and other steppe nomads lived in portable, felt-covered tents called yurts (or gers), which suited their mobile pastoral way of life.

stem: Assertion (A): The Mongol armies were remarkably mobile and effective. Reason (R): They were expert horsemen and archers organised on a disciplined decimal system.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: The Mongol armies' effectiveness came from their expert horsemanship and archery and their organisation into disciplined units on a decimal system (tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands) — R explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): Trade flourished across Eurasia under Mongol rule. Reason (R): The Mongols secured the trade routes and set up a relay/postal system, creating a period of relative peace (Pax Mongolica).
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Trade flourished because the Mongols unified and secured the vast trans-Eurasian routes, established a fast relay/postal system, and maintained relative peace (the Pax Mongolica), which encouraged commerce and exchange — R explains A.

stem: The Mongol relay/postal system for rapid communication across the empire was called the:
solution: The Mongols set up the 'yam', a relay/postal system with stations providing fresh horses and lodging, enabling messengers and officials to travel rapidly across the vast empire.

stem: Genghis Khan is credited with promulgating a code of laws/regulations known as the:
solution: Genghis Khan is credited with promulgating the 'Yasa', a code of laws and regulations that governed the Mongol people and administration, though its exact contents are debated.

stem: Kublai Khan's attempts to invade and conquer which island failed?
solution: Kublai Khan launched two large naval invasions of Japan, both of which failed, partly due to storms (the 'kamikaze' or 'divine winds') that destroyed the Mongol fleets.

stem: After Genghis Khan's death in 1227, the vast Mongol Empire was:
options: Divided among his sons and their descendants into several khanates
solution: After Genghis Khan's death in 1227, the empire was divided among his sons and their descendants into several khanates (the Yuan, Golden Horde, Il-Khanate and Chagatai Khanate), though they initially recognised a Great Khan.

stem: The successor of Genghis Khan as Great Khan, under whom the empire continued to expand, was his son:
solution: Ogodei, a son of Genghis Khan, succeeded him as the Great Khan and continued the expansion of the Mongol empire, including campaigns into Europe and China.

stem: Match the khanate with its region: (i) Yuan (ii) Golden Horde (iii) Il-Khanate — (a) Russia (b) Iran (c) China:
solution: The Yuan dynasty ruled China, the Golden Horde ruled Russia and the western steppes, and the Il-Khanate ruled Iran.

stem: The way of life of the steppe nomads like the Mongols was based mainly on:
solution: The steppe nomads' way of life was based on pastoralism — herding horses, sheep, goats and cattle — and moving seasonally in search of pasture and water, supplemented by hunting and trade.

stem: The Mongols' religion before their later adoption of other faiths was based mainly on:
options: Shamanism and the worship of the sky and nature
solution: The traditional religion of the Mongols was a form of shamanism, involving the worship of the eternal blue sky (Tengri), nature spirits and ancestors, before many later adopted Islam, Buddhism or other faiths.

stem: Genghis Khan's integration of men from different, formerly rival tribes into his army and administration helped to:
options: Break old tribal loyalties and build a unified, loyal following
solution: Genghis Khan deliberately mixed men from different, formerly rival clans and tribes within his army units and administration, breaking old tribal loyalties and forging a new, unified loyalty to himself and the Mongol state.

stem: The Mongols organised their army on a decimal system, with the largest unit of ten thousand being called a:
solution: The Mongol army was organised on a decimal system into units of tens, hundreds, thousands, and ten-thousands; the unit of ten thousand men was called a 'tumen'.

stem: The Mongols' adoption of siege warfare techniques allowed them to:
options: Capture fortified cities, not just win open-field battles
solution: By learning and adopting siege warfare techniques (using catapults, engineers and captured specialists), the Mongols were able to capture strongly fortified cities, greatly extending the range of their conquests.

stem: The Mongol practice of sometimes sparing skilled craftsmen and specialists during conquests shows that they:
options: Valued useful skills and put such people to work in their service
solution: During their conquests, the Mongols often spared skilled craftsmen, artisans and specialists, deporting them to work in Mongol service, because they valued their useful skills for building, administration and warfare.

stem: The trans-Eurasian contact of the Mongol era facilitated the spread of technologies and ideas, such as:
options: Gunpowder, printing and knowledge between East and West
solution: The unification of much of Eurasia under Mongol rule facilitated exchanges across the continent, spreading technologies (like gunpowder, printing, the compass) and knowledge, as well as goods and, at times, diseases, between East and West.

stem: The period of relative peace and stability across Mongol-ruled Eurasia that promoted trade is called the:
solution: The 'Pax Mongolica' ('Mongol Peace') refers to the period of relative stability and security across the Mongol-controlled trade routes of Eurasia, which greatly encouraged long-distance trade and cultural exchange.

stem: The name/title 'Genghis Khan' (Chinggis Khan) is generally taken to mean:
solution: The title 'Genghis Khan' is generally interpreted to mean the 'universal' or 'oceanic' ruler — the supreme and universal sovereign of the Mongols.

stem: Under the Yuan dynasty in China, the Mongols governed by:
options: Making use of Chinese administrative methods while keeping Mongol dominance
solution: As rulers of China, the Mongols of the Yuan dynasty made use of existing Chinese administrative structures and officials while maintaining Mongol control and privileges, adapting to govern a vast settled population.

stem: The Mongol rule over Russia through the Golden Horde is remembered in Russian history as a period of:
solution: Mongol rule over the Russian principalities through the Golden Horde, which lasted a long time, is remembered in Russian history as a period of foreign domination, sometimes called the 'Tatar yoke'.

stem: The decline and break-up of the unified Mongol empire into separate khanates was due partly to:
options: Its vast size, succession disputes, and the assimilation of Mongols into local cultures
External conquest of all khanates at once
solution: The unified Mongol empire fragmented due to its enormous size, disputes over succession among the descendants of Genghis Khan, and the gradual assimilation of the Mongols into the different settled cultures they ruled.

stem: Genghis Khan's campaign against the wealthy Khwarazmian empire (in Central Asia/Iran) was significant because it:
options: Extended Mongol conquests westward with great destruction
solution: Genghis Khan's campaign against the Khwarazmian empire, provoked by the killing of Mongol envoys and merchants, led to the devastating westward expansion of Mongol conquests into Central Asia and Iran.

stem: Genghis Khan died in which year?
solution: Genghis Khan died in 1227, after which the vast empire he had built was divided among his sons and their descendants.

stem: The significance of the Mongol Empire in world history lies partly in that it:
options: Connected the civilisations of Eurasia and promoted exchange across the continent
solution: The Mongol Empire's significance lies in the way it connected the civilisations of Eurasia — East and West — under one broad political umbrella, promoting trade, travel and the exchange of goods, technologies and ideas across the continent.

stem: The trans-Eurasian trade routes that flourished under the Mongols are often collectively called the:
solution: The trans-Eurasian trade routes connecting China with Central Asia, West Asia and Europe, which flourished under Mongol protection, are collectively known as the Silk Route(s).

stem: The overall assessment of the Mongols in the chapter seeks to correct the one-sided image of them as:
options: Merely bloodthirsty destroyers, by also noting their administrative and connecting role
solution: The chapter seeks to correct the one-sided image of the Mongols as merely brutal destroyers, highlighting also their role as empire-builders, administrators, promoters of trade, and connectors of the Eurasian world.

stem: The composition of the Mongol confederation under Genghis Khan included:
options: Diverse tribes and peoples united under Mongol leadership
solution: The Mongol confederation built by Genghis Khan brought together diverse Mongol and Turkic tribes and, over time, many other conquered peoples, all united under Mongol leadership and a common military-political structure.

stem: The study of the Mongols is valuable for world history because it shows:
options: The impact of nomadic peoples on the settled world and the interconnection of Eurasia
solution: Studying the Mongols is valuable because it reveals the significant impact of nomadic steppe peoples on the settled civilisations, and how their vast empire interconnected the different regions and cultures of Eurasia.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Nomadic Empires' is that:
options: The Mongols built a vast empire that connected Eurasia and had lasting historical significance beyond mere destruction
solution: The chapter concludes that the nomadic Mongols, under Genghis Khan and his successors, built one of history's largest empires, which — despite its violence — connected the civilisations of Eurasia, promoted trade and exchange, and left a lasting mark on world history.
